Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM4610 : Biosensor Technology { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Principles of Sensing, Classification and Terminology of Sensors, Measurands. Hall Effect sensors and associated signal conditioning circuits, Sensors for displacement (linear and angular), velocity, acceleration, force, torque, vibration and shock measurements. Sensor measurements for conductivity and viscosity. Fabrication and miniaturization techniques Optical technology and principle of optical measurements. Sensor-to-Frequency Conversion Data-Acquisition Systems: Hardware and Software of Data Acquisition System (DAS), Electronic Interface, Integrated Sensors, Wireless integration. Smart sensor, MEMS and Nano sensor.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the basic principles and classification of senors and measurands
2 .

To know the hardware and software of DAQ system and Electronic Interface systems
3 .

To understand how to measure various parameters and helps to design simple biomedical sensors
4 .

To study about the sensor measurements for biological applications.

After completing the course, the students will able to:
1. Understand the principle of sensors and transducer functioning
2. know the different types of biosensors applied to different biomedical fields
3. know the basics of the hardware and software requirements for the Electronic Interfaces of Sensor
4. Describe the basic concepts of MEMS based smart sensors.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM6401 : Advanced Recombinant DNA Technology { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Recombinant DNA Technology
Brief history of recombinant DNA Technology, Relevance and impact of rDNA technology, Applications of Recombinant DNA Technology including I health, agriculture, food process, environment and energy sectors.
Module 2: Tools used in RDT
Enzymes used in gene manipulation, host systems and, Gene isolation, cloning and expression, DNA sequencing, oligonucleotide synthesis, Southern and Northern hybridization, FISH, PCR, RAPD, RFLP, DNA fingerprinting and their applications for diagnosis of disease,
Module 3: Advanced Techniques in RDT
Site-directed mutagenesis, Gene silencing, Gene transfer technologies, Gene therapy, Functional genomics: DNA chips and microarray gene screen technology transgenic animals and gene knockout techniques. Genome sequencing projects, advancement of genome sequencing using Next generation Sequencing (NGS).
Module 4: Study of emerging genome editing tools
Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) and RNA-guided engineered nucleases (RGENs) derived from the bacterial clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-Cas (CRISPR-associated) system.
Module 5: Ethical and Biosafety Considerations
Ethical issues in RDT, Regulatory frameworks for genetically modified organisms (GMOs), Ethical clearances for recombinant products.

Course Objective

1 .

To gain detailed knowledge about molecular biology
2 .

To learn the real application of RDT in different area
3 .

To learn advancement of the recombinant DNA technology
4 .

To learn ethical issues regarding recombinant products

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Technical skills and knowledge development on versatile techniques in rDNA technology
2. Thorough understanding about the real applications of rDNA Technology
3. Gaining insight in the new advancements of the rDNA techniques and their field of application in real context
4. Expertise in designing and conducting experiments involving genome editing and manipulation
5. Development of awareness related to ethical issues of RDT

Essential Reading

1 .

Brown TA, Gene cloning and DNA analysis, Wiley-Blackwell, USA.

2 .

Primrose SB, Twyman RM, Old RW, Principles of gene manipulation and genomics., Wiley-Blackwell, USA.

Supplementary Reading

2 .

Lewin B., Genes IX, Jones and Bartlett, USA

8597.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA4811 : Human Settlement Planning { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Introduction to the basics of planning concepts:
Definition and concept of planning, planning objectives, role of planners, approaches to planning, types of plans/planning documents (like regional plan, city plan, zoning plan, and local area plan) evolution of human settlement, definition of urban and rural areas, Census classification of urban settlement, urban-rural continuum, urbanisation, urbanism types of regions and regional planning.
Module II: Classification and hierarchy of settlements:
Morphology of cities, classification of urban settlements based on different criteria, metropolitan concept, the concept of primacy, primate cities, Zipf’s Rank Size Rule hierarchy of settlement – introduction to various theories of planning.
Assignment – Application of Zipf’s Rank Size Rule.
Module III: Evolution of settlement planning concepts:
Settlement planning in history – ancient cities, medieval cities and renaissance cities around the globe, ancient Indian villages and towns, Indian cities post Vedic villages, colonial cities in India Modern planning concepts - Ebenezer Howard’s Garden City, the Geddesian Triad, CA Perry’s neighbourhood unit plan, Radburn layout, Radiant city, and Broadacre city models of urban growth – concentric zone theory, sector theory, multiple nuclei theory, and others, introduction to modern city planning in India Emerging concepts in planning - sustainable development goals, green city, green urbanism, inclusive city Transit-oriented development, smart cities, global cities, agile city.
Module IV: Urban Infrastructure Planning:
National Land Utilisation Policy, land reforms in India, zoning and land use classification, development control rules.
Housing: definitions related to housing, housing policies in India
National Urban Transport Policy, traffic, and transportation – hierarchy of roads, road layouts, types of intersection, basic introduction of LOS Desire line diagrams, threshold analysis,
Social Infrastructure – types, hierarchy and calculation
Physical infrastructure – types and calculation.
Assignment – Calculation of social and physical infrastructure, student presentation on various housing policies in India.
Module V: Techniques in planning processes:
Types of data and data collection methods (primary and secondary), types of data measurement scale – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio, understanding variables, tabulation and graphic presentation of data
Sampling techniques, types of surveys (e.g., household survey, volume count survey, aerial survey, satellite images, etc.)
Basic analysis – central tendency, Pearson correlation basic population projection.
Assignment – Collection and representation of time series and cross-sectional data, basic population projection.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the relevance and scope of human settlement planning.
2 .

To familiarize oneself with the historical development of planning and understand its significance for contemporary town planning.
3 .

To familiarize oneself with different domains of planning, planning process and basic techniques.

Course Outcome

1 .

Ability to understand complexity, conflicts, and multi-disciplinary aspects of planning.
Ability to apply the understanding of existing planning theories and solutions.
Ability to incorporate needs of various stakeholders in the planning process.
Ability to design a small neighbourhood or integrated townships.

Essential Reading

1 .

Hall, P., & Tewdwr-Jones, M., Urban and Regional Planning (5th ed.), Abingdon: Routledge

2 .

Levy, J. M., Contemporary urban planning (11th ed.), New York: Routledge

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Hall, P., Cities of tomorrow (3rd ed.), Malden: Blackwell

2 .

Jacobs, J., The death and life of great American cities, New York: Random House

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE6303 : Nonlinear Control { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Syllabus:
Introduction and Mathematical Preliminaries [3 L]: Modeling complex systems as nonlinear systems, motivating examples, detailed discussions on practical nonlinear systems and their salient features, necessary mathematical tools.
Analysis of second order Nonlinear systems [2L]: Phase Plane Analysis techniques, Poincare Bendixon theorem for limit cycle detection.
Stability of equilibrium points and Region of Attractions [10 L]: Lyapunov stability analysis for nonlinear systems, Local and Global Stability, concept of stability basin, Cheatev's Instability Theorem, Condition of linearization and stability analysis of the linearized model near an equilibrium point, invariant set theorems and its importance. Stability analysis of nonautonomous systems, use of comparison lemma to analyze stability,
Mid-Sem
Input-state and Input-output stability [5L]: Boundedness and ultimate boundedness, concept of input to state stability, Input Output Stability Analysis, Introduction to L-P space, L Stability analysis of state models, small gain theorem.
Passivity [4 L]: Memoryless functions and Sector Nonlinearities, PRTF & Lyapunov Feedback systems, Lure’s Problem, Circle & Popov Criteria
Controller Design for Nonlinear Systems [6L]: Normal form, Controller form, Concepts & linearization, Feedback linearization, Sliding Mode Control
End Sem

Course Objective

1 .

Elaborating salient features of the nonlinear differential equations
2 .

Explaining the stability analysis tools of the nonlinear systems.
3 .

Introducing different advanced analysis techniques for nonautonomous nonlinear systems.
4 .

To introduce the design techniques of nonlinear controllers for different complicated dynamical systems.

Course Outcome

1 .

After attending this course, students should be able to:
1) Find out the fixed point of a given nonlinear dynamical system and explore the possibilities of carrying out linear analysis.
2) Analyse the stability of nonlinear systems using LaSalle's invariance theorem and determine the region of attraction for the same.
3) Determine a suitable analysis method for assessing the stability of the autonomous and nonautonomous nonlinear systems
4) Utilize the Lebsigue space concept to analyse the nonlinear systems' stability subject to different excitation signals.
5) Carry out the passivity analysis for a given system.
6) Design nonlinear control law to address the performance issues of complicated nonlinear systems.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME3103 : System Dynamics and Control { 2-0-0 / 2}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I (04 hours): Introduction to control system design, closed loop and open loop system, design principles of control systems, Laplace transforms method transfer functions
Module-2 (6 hours): Block diagrams, deriving transfer functions of physical systems, signal flow graphs proportional, derivation and integral controllers, impulse response functions. First order systems, second order systems, higher order systems
Module-3 (07 hours): Routh's stability criterion, static and dynamic error coefficients, introduction to system optimization. Root locus plots, root locus analysis of control systems, Bode plots, Logarithmic, polar and log magnitude versus phase plots
Module-4 (07 hours): Nyquist stability criterion, stability analysis, closed loop frequency response lag, lead compensations. Nonlinear control systems, describing function analysis of nonlinear control systems.
Module-5 (12 hours): Introduction to discrete time systems, state space representation of systems, Liapunov stability analysis, optimal control systems based on quadratic performance indexes, adaptive control systems, LQR and LQG

Course Objective

1 .

To provide a basic understanding of the concepts and techniques involved in modelling and designing control schemes for dynamic systems
2 .

To introduce the components and their representation of control systems
3 .

To learn various methods for analyzing the time response, frequency response and stability of the systems
4 .

To learn the various approach for the state variable analysis

Course Outcome

1 .

Students will acquire in-depth knowledge of concepts from classical control and modern control theories, understand the concept of transfer function and use it for obtaining system response, analyze dynamic systems for their stability and performance, and design of controllers based on the stability and performance requirements. At the end of the course, the student will be able to:
CO1: Identify the various control system components and their representations
CO2: Analyze the various time domain parameters
CO3: Analysis the various frequency response plots and its system.
CO4: Apply the concepts of various system stability criterions.
CO5: Design various transfer functions of digital control system using state variable models

Essential Reading

1 .

K. Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, PHI

2 .

Gene Franklin, J. D. Powell, and Abbas Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, Prentice Hall

Supplementary Reading

1 .

B. Kuo, Control System Engineering, PHI

2 .

Eronini I. Umez-Eronini, System Dynamics and Control, Thomson Engineering

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH5104 : Introduction to Plasma Physics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

(6 hrs): Definition of plasma, Occurrence of Plasma in nature, Plasma in space: Solar wind and interplanetary medium, Magnetosphere and ionosphere, Plasma parameters, Plasma characterization, Debye Shielding.

Module 2 :

(8 hrs): Charged particle dynamics in time varying fields, Motion of a charged particle in uniform and non-uniform electric & magnetic fields, Magnetic moments and adiabatic invariant.

Module 3 :

(8 hrs): Plasma Oscillations and dispersion relations, Ionic acoustic waves, Alfven waves, magnetosonic waves, two stream and drift instabilities in plasma, Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities, Magnetorotational instability in astrophysical plasmas, nonlinear effects in plasma waves.
Module 4 :

(8 hrs): Magnetic confinement: Tokomaks, Stellarators, Mirror mechanism, instabilities in magnetic confinement devices, concept of laser driven fusion, fusion ignition conditions and compression scheme.

Module 5 :

(6 hours): Plasma Application: Plasma Etching, material processing, plasma coating, plasma propulsion-Hall thrusters and ion thrusters.

Course Objective

1 .

To learn the fundamental properties of plasma.
2 .

To distinguish different types of plasmas found in nature and laboratory.
3 .

To analyze particle motion in electromagnetic fields.
4 .

To develop a theoretical understanding of plasma kinetics & confinement.
5 .

To know the plasma application in material processing, coating & thrusters.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of course, students will be able to:
CO1: understand the fundamental properties of plasma.

2 .

CO2: learn to analyze particle motion in electromagnetic fields .
3 .

CO3: acquire the knowledge plasma oscillations and dispersion relations.

4 .

CO4: understand the concept of Magnetic confinement & fusion ignition conditions.
5 .

CO5: acquire the knowledge of plasma application in different fields.
